extracted.intended_audience: public relations counselors, PR practitioners, journalists, and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations counsel on how to understand, reach, and influence publics via established media by applying group and individual psychology, media-selection practices, and timing. Emphasizes analysis of stereotypes, herd dynamics, and institutional constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist the established point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: “The moulder of public opinion must enlist the established point of view.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR work should align with or enlist already-established viewpoints rather than attempting wholesale rejection of them; the text contrasts the duty to carry news with the possibility of selective action and keeping up community morale (New York Tribune advertisement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain editorial courage despite public hostility
rubrics_metrics.description: “Newspapers have consciously maintained a point of view toward which the public is either hostile or cold.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/publishers may need bravery to stand for policy despite pressure; cited example: the two Baltimore Suns that 'have courageously and consistently stood for the policies of their editors' and refused to yield to pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the press as a vehicle for public campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: The press can originate and carry campaigns that lead to concrete changes (laws, reforms, public action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by multiple World campaigns listed (e.g., disarmament coverage, legislation enacted based on the World’s advocacy, anti-ticket-speculator law, daylight-saving changes, Ku Klux Klan exposés, motor vehicle law changes, Evening World’s coal-price campaign). Shows that newspapers can lead or catalyze public movements when they commit to a campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the mirrors of the public mind (media standards and audiences)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Study of the mirrors of the public mind—the press, the motion pictures, the lecture platform and the others—reveal to him what their standards are and those of the groups they reach.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze each medium’s conventions, moral standards, and the specific audiences it reaches; this informs what content and tone will resonate and what will be ignored or suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know individual and group psychological principles
rubrics_metrics.description: “He must add a thorough knowledge of the principles which govern individual and group action.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR counsel must understand how individuals and groups accept or resist changes in viewpoints—knowledge of psychology is necessary to predict receptivity and to design persuasive approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and account for stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: “Psychological habits, or as Mr. Lippmann calls them, ‘stereotypes’... largely determine what group of facts we shall see and in what light we shall see them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereotypes are shorthand images people use to interpret information; effective messaging must recognize existing stereotypes, choose which to exploit or gently alter, and realize they strongly filter perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for crowd (herd) psychology and its resistance to change
rubrics_metrics.description: The crowd is a 'state of mind' that causes groups to resist fundamental changes; group membership produces 'logic-proof' compartments and strong resistance to contrary standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that group identity creates mechanisms (precedent, authority, habit) that make fundamental change difficult; PR strategies must work with or gradually alter these group mechanisms rather than assuming individuals will reason independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage herd characteristics (homogeneity, suggestibility, leadership susceptibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trotter’s five characteristics of the herd: intolerance/fear of solitude; sensitivity to the voice of the herd; subject to pack/ herd passions; remarkable susceptibility to leadership; relations dependent on recognition as a herd member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these traits deliberately: craft messages that signal belonging, employ recognized leaders, provide herd-sanctioned cues, and avoid isolating target audiences. Recognize homogeneity’s survival value and use group norms to make suggestions acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match cause to existing group reaction and tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: “The cause he represents must have some group reaction and tradition in common with the public he is trying to reach.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attempting persuasion, ensure the campaign aligns with the target group’s traditions, values, or prior reactions; examples: Margaret Sanger’s success/failure depending on audience readiness, Madam Curie’s welcomed visit owing to prior public preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time releases and messages with news context in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: “All the news that a newspaper prints is affected by what else happened that day.” (Tribune advertisement: 'What Else Happened That Day?')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule announcements to avoid being crowded out by bigger events; consider daily and topical news cycles—when 'real news' breaks, semi-news is displaced. Use timing to maximize prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor content to media selection conventions and readership
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every newspaper when it reaches the reader is the result of a whole series of selections... There are no objective standards here. There are conventions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft angles, headlines, and content to fit a publication’s selection habits and the tastes of its readership (examples: New York Sun, New York Evening Post, World). Understand position, space, and emphasis conventions in each outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach the public through established mediums appropriate to heterogeneous audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: “The public can be reached only through established mediums of communication.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a heterogeneous modern society, direct single-person appeals are insufficient; use established channels (press, film, lecture platforms) and experts who know how to reach disparate groups and languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits of PR; it cannot manufacture public opinion out of nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is as untrue to contend that public opinion is manufactured as it is to contend that public opinion governs the agencies which mould it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR can intensify or dissipate existing sympathy but cannot create a sympathetic public where no underlying readiness or need exists; be realistic about attainable change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcome the audience’s internal censorship (biases, 'logic-proof' compartments)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The average citizen is the world’s most efficient censor. His own mind is the greatest barrier between him and the facts. His own ‘logic-proof compartments,’ his own absolutism are the obstacles...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messaging to circumvent or reduce internal filters and preconceptions—use trusted intermediaries, familiar frames, or incremental persuasion rather than frontal assaults on entrenched beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the institutional background and controlling standards of opinion-shaping institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Powerful standards control the very institutions which are supposed to help form public opinion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze institutions (press, schools, churches, motion pictures) to understand the background constraints and standards that shape what they will present; this affects what campaigns can accomplish through those institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an outsider/impartial perspective to avoid group bias
rubrics_metrics.description: “The training of the public relations counsel permits him to step out of his own group to look at a particular problem with the eyes of an impartial observer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practitioners should consciously detach from their own group’s assumptions to evaluate how different target groups will perceive messages; this reduces projection of one’s own stereotypes onto others.
